name: Thirumuruganatheswarar Temple, Thirumuruganpoondi
deity: Shiva as Thirumuruganatheswarar, with the goddess Avudainayagi
period: A Paadal Petra Sthalam of Kongu Nadu, sung by Sundarar in the Tevaram (8th century)
dynasty: Kongu Chola (present structure), with later additions
summary: On the road between Tiruppur and Avinashi, Shiva is worshipped as Thirumuruganatheswarar, the Lord to whom Murugan himself prayed — and the Lord who, in the guise of a hunter, once robbed the saint Sundarar.

sections.history: Thirumuruganpoondi lies in Tiruppur district on the road between Tiruppur and Avinashi, and its Shiva temple is one of the 276 Paadal Petra Sthalams — a Paadal Petra Sthalam of Kongu Nadu, the western upland country of the Tevaram. Sundarar is the saint who sang it, and his pathigam here is unlike most hymns of praise: it is the song of a devotee who has just been robbed, asking his Lord why he dwells in a place where travellers are waylaid. The present stone temple is generally dated to the Kongu Cholas in about the tenth century, and the shrine has been cared for and added to since. Avinashi, another Kongu Nadu shrine sung by Sundarar, is only a few kilometres away.
sections.architecture: The temple is a compact Dravidian shrine, and one feature surprises first-time visitors: there is no towering rajagopuram at its entrance, a rare absence among the great temples of Tamil Nadu. Within, the lingam of Thirumuruganatheswarar stands in the main sanctum, with the goddess Avudainayagi in her own shrine. The inner mandapam holds an image of Shiva as the hunter, and Sundarar appears twice — once with a sorrowful face, once rejoicing. The temple has three sacred springs: the Shanmuga theertham at the centre, with the Gnana and Brahma theerthams on either side.
sections.legends: The temple's name remembers Murugan. Tradition says that after slaying the demon Surapadman, he bore the stain of that killing and came here to install and worship a lingam, and was freed of it — so Shiva is the Lord whom Murugan worshipped. A square stone beneath the neem tree outside is pointed out as the sin he left behind. The best-loved story belongs to Sundarar: returning from the Chera country laden with gifts, he was waylaid by Shiva in the form of a hunter and stripped of everything, until his sorrowful pathigam won it all back.
sections.festivals: The temple's own festival is the Vedupari utsavam, when the robbery of Sundarar by the hunter-Lord is re-enacted each year and the procession carries the story through the town. Maha Shivaratri, the monthly Pradosham and the festivals of Murugan are also kept with devotion; confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: Pilgrims come here to pray for release from old burdens, as Murugan did. The Shanmuga theertham carries a story of its own: tradition says the childless Pandya king Maharadhan bathed in it and offered payasam made with its water, and was blessed with children. Look for the two faces of Sundarar — grief and joy — and then continue to the Avinashi temple close by.

visit.timings: Open daily in morning and evening sessions with a midday closure, as at most Kongu Nadu temples. Confirm current timings locally before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left outside before entering. Follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.photography: Photography is not permitted inside the sanctum; in the outer areas, ask the temple staff before taking pictures, especially of rituals.
visit.gettingThere: Thirumuruganpoondi is about 9 km from Tiruppur on the Tiruppur–Avinashi road, and about 5 km short of Avinashi; town buses on this route stop near the temple. Tiruppur is the nearest railway station, and Coimbatore International Airport is roughly 45 km away by road.
